    14. Dense subclasses of #

    In Corollary 11.14 and Theorem 12.5, we established that is a complete normed space for every . Its elements are equivalence classes of functions that agree almost everywhere. A statement about all functions in therefore cannot be verified by evaluating the functions at points, and we ask how such a statement can be proved.

    Let us consider an example on with Lebesgue measure. Suppose that , and translate the graph of to the right by a small distance . Does tend to as ? If is continuous and vanishes outside a bounded interval, the answer is yes: is uniformly continuous, so is small for all simultaneously, and integrating over a bounded interval that contains the supports of both functions gives . This argument does not apply to , for which at points close to and to . Suppose, however, that for every there is such a continuous function with . A translation does not change the norm, so Minkowski’s inequality gives The answer for thus implies the answer for .

    The argument requires that every function in can be approximated in the norm by functions of a smaller class, on which the statement can be verified directly. A class with this property is called dense. In these notes, we first approximate functions in by simple functions, then by continuous functions, and on by continuous functions with compact support. We then return to translations, and we prove in the same way that convolutions of functions in and are continuous.

    After studying these notes, you will be able to do the following.

    • Approximate a function in by simple functions that vanish outside a set of finite measure, and explain why this approximation fails in .

    • Approximate a Borel set by closed and open sets with respect to a finite Borel measure on a metric space, and by compact sets on .

    • Construct continuous functions that approximate the indicator of a closed set in , and prove that bounded continuous functions are dense in for a finite Borel measure on a metric space.

    • Prove that is dense in for Borel measures that are finite on compact sets, and give examples where this density fails.

    • Prove a statement for all functions in by density: the continuity of translations, its failure to be uniform, and the continuity of convolution on .

    Throughout these notes, unless a smaller range or is stated explicitly, and functions are measurable functions with values in . A subset is dense in if for every and every there exists with .

    14.1 Density of simple functions#

    The Lebesgue integral of a non-negative function is computed by approximating the function from below by simple functions. We now show that the same approximation converges in . A simple function is a measurable function that takes finitely many values. Writing for its distinct non-zero values and , we have the canonical representation with pairwise disjoint measurable sets , and For , a simple function therefore belongs to if and only if each has finite measure, that is, if and only if . We denote by the set of simple functions with .

    14.2 Approximation of Borel sets by closed and open sets#

    Simple functions take finitely many values, but their level sets are arbitrary measurable sets. To approximate them by continuous functions, we need a relation between measurable sets and continuity, and therefore a distance on .

Continuous functions are Borel measurable (Theorem 6.11). We denote by the bounded continuous functions on . If is finite and , then , so .

    Suppose that we wish to approximate a function in by continuous functions. By Theorem 14.1, it is enough to approximate simple functions, and hence indicators of Borel sets. A continuous function makes the transition from on to away from on a region around , and the error in is bounded by the measure of this region. For a closed set , the points at distance less than from form an open set that decreases to as , so the transition can be made on a set of small measure. For a general Borel set , we first replace by a closed subset of almost the same measure. The next theorem provides this subset, together with an open set that contains and has almost the same measure.

    14.3 Density of continuous functions#

    We now combine the approximation by simple functions with the regularity of the measure.

    Theorem 14.5 (Density of continuous functions for finite Borel measures)#

    For a finite Borel measure on a metric space and , the set is dense in .

    The proof passes through three classes of functions. By Theorem 14.1, every is an limit of simple functions with Borel sets . By inner regularity (Theorem 14.3), each can be replaced by a closed subset of almost the same measure, which yields a simple function whose level sets are closed. Finally, each indicator of a closed set is approximated by continuous functions. In the last two reductions, the quasi-triangle inequality reduces the approximation of a linear combination to the approximation of a single indicator.

    14.4 Density of compactly supported continuous functions#

    Lebesgue measure on is not finite, so Theorem 14.5 does not apply to it directly. A Borel measure that is finite on compact sets is finite on every ball, so its restriction to a ball is a finite Borel measure. We combine truncation to a large ball with the approximations of the previous two sections. For , the support is the closure of , and denotes the continuous functions with compact support.     14.5 Proofs by density#

    We return to the question of the introduction. A proof by density establishes a property for every in two steps. We first verify the property for the functions of a dense class. We then pass to the limit, which requires an estimate for the error: replacing by a function of the class changes the quantity under study by at most a constant multiple of . We carry out two such proofs. For translations, we approximate one function, and for convolutions, we approximate both factors.

    In this section, unless stated otherwise, carries Lebesgue measure , and . Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives for every measurable and : the identity holds for indicators, then for non-negative simple functions, and then for by monotone convergence. In the same way, .
